speaker: Raquel Urtasun
title: An AI-First Approach to Enable Self Driving at Scale, with Raquel Urtasun of Waabi
question: In autonomous driving, why does treating end-to-end AI as a pure black box trained on driving examples fail to reach real-world deployment?
guest: An alternative that you might think of is, why don't we use AI in order to automate this process? Now, if you look at current approaches that utilize AI, the problem is that typically they think about AI as a black box, that if you give the system enough examples, it's gonna learn to handle all the possible situations. Unfortunately, there are two issues with this approach. There is the fact that you're gonna need too many examples, and in particular, you need to observe all these rare situations in order to be able to handle them. And this is not necessarily something that you might be able to do or that it might be ethical to actually do. Some of those situations might finish in a collision, for example. On top of this, there is no interpretability if you treat the AI system just as a black box, so it's gonna be very difficult to impossible to also verify the system. So this is something that regulators are not gonna feel comfortable with, in terms of approving such a system to be deployed in the real world.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
A pure black box trained by imitating driving examples fails mainly because it cannot be shown to be safe, and because imitation alone does not generalize to the situations that matter most.

Driving is dominated by a long tail of rare events. Demonstration data is overwhelmingly routine driving, so the model sees few crashes, near-misses, or odd edge cases, and it never sees how to recover from its own mistakes. Small errors then compound: once the car drifts into states unlike the training data, its behaviour becomes unpredictable (covariate shift). Imitation also learns correlations rather than causes, so a model may latch onto shortcuts, such as braking because the car ahead brakes rather than because the light is red.

The second problem is verification. Without interpretable intermediate outputs, engineers cannot diagnose failures, fix one specific behaviour without retraining and revalidating everything, or build the safety case that regulators and standards require. Open-loop metrics also poorly predict closed-loop driving.

Deployed systems therefore add structure: intermediate perception and prediction representations, explicit safety rules or fallback layers, closed-loop simulation, and targeted testing.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: Treating end-to-end autonomous driving as a pure black box trained on driving examples fails to reach real-world deployment because passive imitation cannot guarantee closed-loop safety, interpretability, or long-tail reliability. Models trained solely on human demonstrations learn statistical correlations rather than causal physics or traffic rules, inviting causal confusion and covariate shift: when minor control deviations nudge the vehicle into states absent from normal driving logs, errors rapidly compound without learned recovery behaviors. Moreover, routine demonstrations overwhelmingly reflect uneventful driving and lack the rare, safety-critical edge cases where unconstrained neural networks can hallucinate or act unpredictably. Because a pure black box maps raw sensor inputs directly to actuation without structured intermediate representations, engineers cannot isolate whether perception, prediction, or planning caused a failure, and fixing one issue via retraining risks silent regressions elsewhere. Finally, opaque networks cannot enforce hard physical or legal bounds, precluding the deterministic safety guardrails, formal verification, and regulatory assurance required for driverless operation.

noweb.answer:
Treating end-to-end autonomous driving as a pure black box trained solely on human demonstrations fails because passive imitation breaks down in closed-loop execution and cannot provide verifiable safety guarantees. Because training logs overwhelmingly capture safe expert behavior, minor control errors during live driving push the vehicle into unfamiliar states where mistakes rapidly compound—a problem known as covariate shift. Purely observational learning also suffers from causal confusion, latching onto spurious correlations rather than true physical hazards, while remaining brittle across the long tail of rare, life-critical edge cases scarcely present in everyday traffic data. 

Just as critically, an opaque mapping from raw sensor inputs to steering and braking makes system maintenance and certification intractable. Without interpretable intermediate representations, closed-loop feedback, or explicit safety guardrails, engineers cannot isolate whether a dangerous maneuver stemmed from faulty perception or flawed planning, fix specific bugs without triggering unpredictable regressions elsewhere, or enforce hard physical bounds on worst-case behavior to satisfy regulators and public trust.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Pure black-box imitation learning breaks down because driving safety is decided by the long tail. The rare, dangerous situations that matter most, such as unusual road users, odd construction zones or sensor glitches, barely show up in the demonstration data. Behavior cloning also suffers from compounding errors and distribution shift. Once the car drifts slightly away from the states its human examples covered, it meets situations it never learned how to recover from. Models can pick up shortcuts too, copying correlations in the data, like braking because the car ahead brakes, instead of the real cause.

A monolithic network also gives engineers nothing to look into. When it fails, you can't easily tell whether perception, prediction or planning was at fault. You can't check its behavior against rules or safety constraints, and you can't show regulators a convincing safety case. Validating it statistically would take billions of miles.

That's why deployed systems such as Waymo, Tesla FSD v12+ and Wayve add structure. They use intermediate representations you can inspect, auxiliary perception tasks, safety layers or guardrails, closed-loop simulation and reinforcement learning, and targeted mining of edge cases. models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Treating autonomous driving as a pure black box trained on driving examples fails to reach real-world deployment because driving is a safety-critical domain dominated by rare, long-tail edge cases. Models trained strictly by imitating human demonstrations suffer from covariate shift—where minor errors compound and push the vehicle into unfamiliar states—and causal confusion, latching onto spurious correlations rather than true traffic physics and rules. Even more critically, a monolithic black box lacks interpretability and modular debuggability. When a dangerous failure occurs, engineers cannot isolate whether perception, prediction, or planning broke down, nor can they apply targeted fixes without risking regressions elsewhere during retraining. Finally, real-world deployment demands formal safety guarantees, strict adherence to traffic laws, and regulatory certification. Because an opaque neural network cannot provide provable safety bounds and statistical validation alone would require an infeasible number of real-world miles after every update, deployable systems pair learned models with structured intermediate representations, explicit safety guardrails, and verifiable planning constraints.

A black-box model trained to imitate driving examples can perform well on familiar roads and still fail in rare situations that matter most for safety. The training data may contain few examples of a construction worker waving traffic through a red light, for instance. And once the model makes a small mistake, it can put the car in a situation that human drivers in the training data rarely encountered, making further errors more likely.

Deployment also requires evidence that the system can operate safely within defined conditions and respond safely when it reaches its limits. Average performance on recorded drives says little about those limits, and an opaque failure is harder to diagnose and fix. End-to-end learning can still be part of a deployable system, but it needs closed-loop testing, targeted evaluation of rare hazards, and safeguards that can intervene or bring the vehicle to a safe state.

Driving examples show what a driver did in a particular situation. They rarely show what would have happened if the driver had acted differently or how to recover from a mistake the driver never made. Once the AI controls the car, even a small steering error can put it in a position its training data barely covers. Rare hazards are harder still. A model can perform well on millions of ordinary miles while relying on a visual cue that fails in one critical situation.

The deployment problem is showing that the car is safe within the conditions where it will operate. Average accuracy on recorded drives tells little about how the system will respond when its own actions change what happens next. End-to-end learning can be part of a deployed system, but it needs closed-loop testing, targeted evaluation of rare hazards, and a way to reach a safe state when it encounters conditions beyond its capabilities.
